chunks.text: In the summer of 1858, London smelled so bad it got its own name: the Great Stink.
For years, the city's toilets and drains had emptied straight into the River Thames.
Then came a heatwave. The river baked, and the smell drifted everywhere.
The worst spot? Parliament, right on the riverbank.
Lawmakers soaked the curtains in chemicals to block the smell. It didn't work.
Back then, many people thought bad smells spread diseases like cholera.
A doctor named John Snow had shown that cholera actually spread through dirty water. But few listened.
Now, with their own noses suffering, Parliament moved fast. A big sewer plan became law in about eighteen days.
Engineer Joseph Bazalgette built giant tunnels to carry the waste away from the city, plus about eleven hundred miles of street sewers.
The pipes were hidden under brand new riverside embankments.
Much of his system still works under London today.
